title: Tisha B'Av
hook: on the ninth of Av, Jews mourn the destruction of the Temples and read Lamentations

segments.voice: Yesterday, birds, lilies and the line sufficient unto the day. Your line was today is enough. A week's end, too: mourners let in, hesed, Chiron, not punishment, not numb, today is enough. Now, days set aside for mourning. Day seven hundred forty-nine.
screen: `TODAY IS ENOUGH.` · `A WEEK OF PRACTICES FOR HARD DAYS.`

segments.voice: A summer evening. In a synagogue the lights are low. Some people are sitting on the floor or on low stools, the way mourners sit at a shiva. Nobody greets each other with the usual warmth. Someone begins to read from a short book of poems, in a slow, falling chant. The first word is a cry: how. On this one day of the year, a whole community sits like a family at a funeral, for a loss that happened long before anyone in the room was born. The day is called Tisha B'Av.
screen: `LIGHTS LOW, PEOPLE ON THE FLOOR.` → `A SLOW, FALLING CHANT.` → `A FUNERAL FOR A CITY.`

segments.voice: First, the date. Tisha B'Av names a day on the Jewish calendar, the ninth of the month of Av. The Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish teaching, lists the calamities tradition remembers on that day, among them the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem, the first time and the second. It is kept as a fast. Second, the book. The reading is Lamentations, short poems of grief for Jerusalem. A few days ago we heard a turn in its third chapter; this reading starts at the very beginning. Its Hebrew name is its first word, Eikhah: how. In the King James Bible it opens, "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow!" Your line today says it in plain modern words: how lonely sits the city. Third, the picture. The poet doesn't describe rubble. The city becomes a woman sitting alone, a widow, weeping in the night with no one to comfort her. Grief that is too big for a list of facts gets a body and a face. That may be why the book still works: a person can sit beside a person. Fourth, the ending. The last chapter turns to a plea: "Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old." Then one more verse, bitter, about being rejected. In the synagogue, the custom is to repeat the plea for renewal after it, so the reading does not end in the dark. Nothing is fixed. Nobody pretends the loss didn't happen. But the community grieves out loud, together, on a set day, and then rises from the floor.
screen: `THE NINTH OF AV, A DAY OF FASTING.` · `EIKHAH: HOW.` · `THE CITY AS A WIDOW.` · `RENEW OUR DAYS AS OF OLD.` · then, large: `HOW LONELY SITS THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow!" Read it once more, slowly, aloud or under your breath. Then sit with it. Let it stand for whatever it stands for today: a place you lost, a home that changed, a loss people around you carry. Or simply honor that a people has read these words in grief for a very long time. No need to fix anything. Sit beside it. The bell holds the time.
Tisha B'Av: the ninth of Av, the Jewish day of mourning for the Temples, when Lamentations is read low and slow. Today's word.
Your line: how lonely sits the city. Today, read one verse of Lamentations, and let grief have a set place instead of everywhere. Day seven hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: On Tisha B'Av, observant Jews fast, sit low as mourners do, and hear Lamentations (Eikhah) chanted in the synagogue; the plea 'renew our days as of old' is repeated at the end of the reading.

trapdoor: what you thought: Tisha B'Av is just a date on the Jewish calendar.
what it means: a fast day of mourning for the Temples, when Lamentations is chanted by people sitting low.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Taanit 4:6 on the calamities of the ninth of Av; the book's Hebrew name, Eikhah, is its first word.

notes: Quoted from KJV rather than JPS 1917 (wording of 1:1 is near-identical in both); a Judaism Keeper may prefer JPS 1917. Swap if so.
'Five short poems': Lamentations has five chapters; confirm calling them five poems is acceptable.
Customs (sitting on the floor or low stools, low lights, no usual greetings, fasting, repeating 5:21 after 5:22) described generally; confirm wording and that it doesn't overstate uniformity.
Carry 'how lonely sits the city' is the index's modern rendering of Eikhah 1:1, not a quotation of a PD translation; presented as 'plain modern words'.
Mishnah Taanit 4:6 paraphrased: confirm it lists the first and second Temple destructions among the calamities of the ninth of Av.
Hebrew title Eikhah = first word 'how': confirm transliteration (Eikhah/Eicha).
Original תִּשְׁעָה בְּאָב: confirm pointing and pronunciation.
Editor: cut the count 'five' from 'five short poems' (claims rule); added a line acknowledging day 744's use of Lamentations 3 so the book's return reads as deliberate.
